introduction-the-lego-bricks-of-kubernet.core: Kubernetes is a declarative system: you submit desired state as API objects (Pods, Services, Deployments, ConfigMaps, Secrets), and controllers continuously reconcile actual state toward it. A handful of primitives compose into almost every application architecture.

first_principles.problem: Engineers write imperative scripts to start, restart and scale containers by hand.

analogy.title: Lego bricks with a self-repairing model
analogy.story: You describe the model; if a brick falls off, it snaps back automatically.
analogy.breaks: Lego doesn't rebuild itself; Kubernetes controllers do, continuously.

check.a: Controllers continuously compare actual state with desired state and act to close the gap.

pods-the-atomic-unit.core: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share a network namespace (same IP and ports, localhost between them), can share volumes, and are scheduled together onto one node. Pods are ephemeral and replaceable; you rarely create them directly.

first_principles.problem: A team puts a web server and its log shipper in separate Pods and can't share files or localhost.
derivation: Put **tightly coupled** containers in one Pod.

analogy.title: A shared flat
analogy.story: Flatmates share an address and kitchen, but each has their own room.
analogy.breaks: Flatmates move out separately; containers in a Pod are scheduled and removed together.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shipper reads nginx logs from the shared volume.

code.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: web}
spec:
  volumes: [{name: logs, emptyDir: {}}]
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    volumeMounts: [{name: logs, mountPath: /var/log/nginx}]
  - name: shipper
    image: fluent/fluent-bit
    volumeMounts: [{name: logs, mountPath: /logs}]

check.q: How do two containers in one Pod communicate over the network?
check.a: Via localhost, since they share a network namespace.

pod-lifecycle-and-probes.core: Pods move through phases (Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed). Probes tell Kubernetes about container health: startupProbe protects slow starters, readinessProbe controls whether a Pod receives Service traffic, and livenessProbe restarts containers that are stuck. Misconfigured probes cause restart loops or traffic to unready Pods.

first_principles.problem: A Java app is killed by its liveness probe before it finishes starting, looping forever.
truths: Running isn't the same as ready.
Restarts fix deadlocks, not dependency outages.

analogy.title: A restaurant opening routine
analogy.story: The 'open' sign goes up only when the kitchen is ready (readiness); if the chef faints, someone replaces them (liveness).
analogy.breaks: Restaurants can partially open; readiness is binary per Pod.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 150 s to start; traffic only when ready.

code.text:
startupProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 5
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 8080}
  periodSeconds: 5
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3

check.q: Why shouldn't a liveness probe check a database connection?
check.a: A DB outage would restart every Pod in a loop without fixing anything.

services-stable-networking-for-unstable-.core: Pods come and go with changing IPs. A Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name, selects Pods by label, and load-balances across ready endpoints (tracked in EndpointSlices). kube-proxy (iptables/IPVS) or eBPF implements the virtual IP on each node.

first_principles.problem: Clients hard-code Pod IPs that change after every restart.
truths: Only ready Pods should get traffic.
derivation: Use **headless Services** for direct Pod discovery.

analogy.title: A company switchboard number
analogy.story: Callers dial one number; it rings whichever staff member is available.
analogy.breaks: Switchboards route by availability; Services load-balance roughly randomly per connection.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: http://api reaches any ready api Pod.

check.q: What does a headless Service (clusterIP: None) provide?
check.a: DNS records pointing directly at individual Pod IPs instead of a single virtual IP.

service-types-exposing-your-app.core: ClusterIP (default) exposes a Service inside the cluster. NodePort opens a port (30000–32767) on every node. LoadBalancer provisions a cloud load balancer that targets the Service. ExternalName returns a CNAME to an external host. For HTTP, most apps use ClusterIP Services behind an Ingress or Gateway.

first_principles.problem: Every service gets its own cloud LoadBalancer, costing hundreds a month and multiplying public endpoints.
truths: Internal traffic doesn't need public exposure.
HTTP routing can share one entry point.
derivation: **LoadBalancer** for TCP/UDP or single public services.

analogy.title: Doors to a building
analogy.story: Internal doors (ClusterIP), a side door on every floor (NodePort), the main entrance with a receptionist (LoadBalancer).
analogy.breaks: Buildings have one main entrance; each LoadBalancer Service creates another.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One public LB for HTTP instead of ten.

check.q: Which Service type provisions a cloud load balancer?

deployments-managing-stateless-apps.core: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which keep N identical Pods running. Changing the Pod template creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts Pods over, keeping history for rollbacks. Deployments are the standard for stateless apps, combined with HPA for scaling and PDBs for availability.

first_principles.problem: A team runs Pods directly and nothing restarts them when a node dies.

analogy.title: A franchise manager keeping N shops open
analogy.story: If one closes, another opens; when the menu changes, shops are converted one by one.
analogy.breaks: Franchises convert shops slowly; Deployments roll out in seconds to minutes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Instant rollback to the last good version.

code.text:
kubectl set image deploy/web web=web:2.0
kubectl rollout status deploy/web
kubectl rollout undo deploy/web   # back to previous ReplicaSet

check.q: What happens when you change a Deployment's Pod template?
check.a: A new ReplicaSet is created and Pods shift to it according to the rollout strategy.

rolling-updates-zero-downtime.core: RollingUpdate replaces Pods gradually: maxSurge sets how many extra Pods can be created, and maxUnavailable how many can be down during the update. With readiness probes, graceful shutdown (preStop + SIGTERM handling) and connection draining, users see no errors. Recreate kills all old Pods first (downtime).

first_principles.problem: Deploys cause brief 502s because old Pods die before load balancers stop sending them traffic.
truths: New Pods must be ready before old ones leave.
derivation: Add **preStop sleep** (5–10 s) for endpoint propagation.

analogy.title: Replacing lanes on a busy motorway
analogy.story: Open the new lane before closing the old one, and wait for traffic to clear.
analogy.breaks: Drivers see lane signs instantly; endpoint changes take seconds to reach every proxy.

code.text:
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0}
template:
  spec:
    terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
    containers:
    - name: web
      lifecycle: {preStop: {exec: {command: ["sleep", "10"]}}}

check.a: To give endpoint and load balancer updates time to stop sending traffic before the app shuts down.

configmaps-and-secrets-decoupling-config.core: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration and Secrets hold sensitive data (base64-encoded, not encrypted by default), so the same image runs in every environment with different config. Protect Secrets with encryption at rest (KMS provider), RBAC and, ideally, external secret stores (External Secrets Operator, CSI Secrets Store).

first_principles.problem: Database passwords are baked into images and differ per environment, forcing separate builds.
derivation: Sync from **Vault/Secrets Manager** with External Secrets.

analogy.title: A recipe card separate from the kitchen
analogy.story: The same kitchen cooks different dishes depending on the card handed in.
analogy.breaks: Recipe cards are visible; Secrets need extra controls because base64 is readable.

example.title: External secret

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Secret synced from AWS Secrets Manager; never in Git.

example.outcome: one image, many environments, safe secrets.

check.q: Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted by default?
check.a: No; they're base64-encoded, so enable encryption at rest and restrict access.

consuming-configmaps-and-secrets.core: Pods consume ConfigMaps and Secrets as environment variables (env, envFrom) or as files via volume mounts. Mounted files update automatically when the object changes (after a short delay, except with subPath), while environment variables are fixed at container start. Apps must reload files or Pods must restart to pick up changes.

first_principles.problem: A config change is applied but the app keeps using old values.
truths: Env vars are read at process start.
Mounted volumes are refreshed by the kubelet.
derivation: Use **volume mounts** for files and live updates.
Prefer **immutable ConfigMaps** for safety and performance.

analogy.title: A printed handout versus a noticeboard
analogy.story: The handout (env var) doesn't change after it's given out; the noticeboard (mounted file) is updated in place.
analogy.breaks: People read noticeboards when they walk past; apps must actively re-read files.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Config change → new Pod template → rollout.

code.text:
template:
  metadata:
    annotations:
      checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}

check.q: Why don't ConfigMap updates reach environment variables in running Pods?
check.a: Environment variables are set when the container starts and aren't refreshed.
